title: API Inspector Training in the Mountain & Plains States
description: API exam prep for Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, North Dakota and the Permian: mid-size refineries, Cushing tankage and gas plants.
h1: API inspector training for the Mountain and Plains states: mid-size refineries, the Cushing tank hub and oilfield plants
html:
Between the Permian Basin and the Canadian border, API inspection work is spread thin over long distances. The refineries are mid-sized and far apart, the delivery point for the main US crude futures contract is a tank hub in a small Oklahoma town, and much of the equipment belongs to gathering systems and gas plants rather than refineries. Inspectors here drive a lot, cover several sites and often work for small contract inspection firms. This page is for candidates in Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, North Dakota and West Texas who want to sit API 510, API 570, API 580 or API 653. It maps the employers by sub-region, explains what the local crudes and climates demand, covers the practical problem of reaching a test centre, and shows how Atlantis's self-paced online course fits a working life spent between sites.

Oklahoma and Kansas: refineries close to Cushing

Several of the region's refineries cluster within a few hours' drive of Cushing, which is the delivery point for West Texas Intermediate crude futures and a hub of large crude tanks owned by pipeline and storage companies.

  • Tulsa: HF Sinclair lists Tulsa among its refining facilities.
  • Ponca City: Phillips 66's Ponca City refinery was listed at 208,000 barrels a day in early 2023.
  • Wynnewood: CVR Energy's refinery, about 65 miles south of Oklahoma City, has a nameplate capacity of 74,500 barrels a day and makes gasoline, diesel including renewable diesel, military jet fuel, solvents and asphalt.
  • Coffeyville, Kansas: CVR's full-coking, medium-sour crude refinery, rated at 132,000 barrels a day, about 100 miles from Cushing.
  • El Dorado and McPherson, Kansas: HF Sinclair lists El Dorado among its facilities, and CHS's McPherson refinery runs mostly on crude from Kansas producers.

For Cushing itself, the useful fact for a candidate is the regulatory one. Oklahoma's aboveground storage tank rules, at OAC 165:26, adopt API Standard 653, Fifth Edition, by reference, and they exclude all tanks used in the exploration or production of oil and gas. Where a Cushing tank is a breakout tank on a pipeline system, federal rules at 49 CFR 195.432 require inspection according to API 653 and do not allow its risk-based method to set the internal inspection interval. Atlantis's Cushing RBI page explains how that boundary affects a tank-farm programme.

The Front Range and the Salt Lake valley

Colorado's refining is concentrated in one plant. Suncor's Commerce City refinery processes about 103,000 barrels a day, describes itself as the largest refinery in the Rocky Mountain region, buys crude from the Denver-Julesburg Basin and supplies about a third of Denver International Airport's jet fuel along with most of the state's paving-grade asphalt.

Utah's refining sits in one valley. The Utah Office of Energy Development reports five refineries, all in the Salt Lake City area, able to process nearly 209,000 barrels of crude a day between them. Marathon's Salt Lake City refinery is rated at 70,000 barrels a day, HF Sinclair's Woods Cross refinery in West Bountiful at 45,000, and Chevron also refines there. Woods Cross runs regional sweet and waxy crude oils as well as Canadian crude, and waxy crude has consequences an inspector should understand: it is stored and moved warm, so heated tanks, steam or electric tracing on lines and the insulation over them all become part of the inspection picture.

Montana, Wyoming and North Dakota

Billings has two refineries: Phillips 66's, listed at 66,000 barrels a day in early 2023, and the former ExxonMobil refinery that Par Pacific took over in June 2023. CHS's refinery at nearby Laurel relies on Canadian crude and supplies the northern tier states. In Wyoming, HF Sinclair lists facilities at Casper and Sinclair, and its Cheyenne plant was converted in 2021 into a renewable diesel unit processing soybean oil and animal fats, which still needs vessel, piping and tank inspection in its new service. In North Dakota, Marathon's Mandan refinery runs about 72,000 barrels a calendar day, mostly sweet North Dakota crude.

A converted plant such as Cheyenne is a good reminder that API 510 and API 570 are not just about crude oil. A change of service brings new damage mechanisms and often a rerating, and both codes require the inspector to deal with that formally.

The oilfield: gas plants, gathering and tank batteries

West Texas and the Bakken employ many inspectors who never set foot in a refinery. In the Permian, midstream companies including Targa Resources, Enterprise Products, Energy Transfer, Kinetik, EnLink and Brazos Midstream have been adding gas processing plants to keep up with production. In the Bakken, Hess Midstream's Tioga Gas Plant was expanded in 2021 to 400,000 Mcf a day, with tankage for propane, butane and natural gasoline, and its Little Missouri Four plant is a joint venture operated by Targa.

Gas plants are pressure vessel and piping work: inlet separators, amine contactors and regenerators, dehydration, cryogenic expanders and NGL storage. API RP 571 describes the damage those units are prone to, including amine stress corrosion cracking and wet hydrogen sulfide damage. It sits in the API 510 and API 570 bodies of knowledge, though only listed sections are examined, and cryogenic sections raise the low-temperature and impact-test questions that Section VIII expects a vessel inspector to handle.

Tank batteries are a different matter. Production tanks are commonly built to API Specification 12F, for shop-welded tanks, or 12D, for field-welded tanks, both written for storing production liquids. They are not API 650 tanks, and Oklahoma's tank rules exclude exploration and production tanks altogether. An operator may still choose to apply API 653 methods to its field tanks, but a candidate whose working life is tank batteries should know that API 653 is written for tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, API 12C.

What the work here demands of an API inspector

Three themes run through the region. The first is crude quality. Medium-sour crude at plants such as Coffeyville, and sour gas at many field plants, brings wet hydrogen sulfide damage into the vessel programme, so an API 510 candidate from the region should be comfortable with what API RP 571 says about it and with how it affects inspection planning. The second is temperature. Plants in Montana and North Dakota see long, hard winters, while waxy crude in Utah is kept warm in heated tanks and traced lines, and both extremes affect insulation, tracing and corrosion under insulation. The third is distance. Small inspection firms send one inspector to several sites in a week, so that person has to be competent across vessels, piping and tanks rather than in one specialty.

Worked example: minimum shell thickness for a large crude tank

API 653 gives a formula for the minimum acceptable thickness of an entire shell course: t-min equals 2.6 times (H minus 1) times D times G, divided by S times E, where H is the liquid height in feet above the bottom of the course, D the nominal diameter in feet, G the specific gravity, S the allowable stress from the standard's table for the plate material and course, and E the joint efficiency. Take a 120-foot crude tank whose lowest course sees a fill height of 40 feet, storing crude with a specific gravity of 0.85, and assume an allowable stress of 26,000 psi and a joint efficiency of 1.0 for this illustration. The result is 2.6 times 39 times 120 times 0.85, divided by 26,000, which is about 0.40 inch. If the averaged thickness that API 653 calls for on that course comes out at 0.43 inch, it meets t-min, subject to the standard's separate checks on isolated pits and on the corrosion expected before the next inspection. Fill the same tank higher or switch it to a heavier product and the calculation must be repeated. On the exam, the work is in reading S, E and H correctly from the code, not in the arithmetic.

Reaching a test centre from a rural site

API 510, API 570 and API 653 must be taken in person at a Prometric test centre; API's scheduling page lists API 580 among the exams available by remote proctoring. In this region the nearest centre can be a long drive, and seats within a window are allocated first-come, first-served, so a candidate in Williston, Casper or Billings should book as soon as the exam authorisation arrives. API's page also says it may arrange a special testing site if at least 50 applicants do not have a testing centre within 200 miles. Prometric's locator shows the current sites, so check the drive time from your base before you choose one.

Keeping the certificate once you have it

Recertification matters more than usual for inspectors who spend years at remote sites. Each API 510, API 570 or API 653 certificate lasts three years. The recertification application opens 90 days ahead of the expiry date, and API allows a further 90 days after it, at a late fee. Avoiding a resit of the full examination depends on showing that a fifth or more of your working time across those three years went on performing or supervising inspection of the equipment concerned, plus 24 hours of professional development in each cycle, drawn from two or more categories. A web quiz on code changes is added every second cycle, that is every six years; API describes it as 25 open-book questions in four hours, with up to three pauses allowed. Inspectors who move from a refinery into a gas plant or a tank-battery role should check early whether their new work still counts towards the 20 percent.

Studying while covering sites across several states

Because the course is self-paced and online, a candidate can study in a motel room, at a field office or at home between rotations, and pick up where they left off. An instructor answers questions on the codes and calculations as they come up. Inspectors working rotations often get on best by setting a fixed amount of code reading for each day off and saving practice papers for the longer breaks. Before you book, read the eligibility rules on the certification pages: API counts experience gained in the last ten years while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency, with the amount depending on education. Field technicians, NDT technicians with contract inspection firms, plant operators moving into inspection roles and engineers in midstream integrity groups all have routes. See the API 510, API 570 and API 653 certification pages for detail.

Employers sponsoring inspectors in the region

Refiners, midstream operators and small inspection firms in the region can sponsor one inspector or a group, and fees are quoted on request. American Petroleum Institute rules apply to each candidate individually: API administers the examination, sets eligibility and issues the certification, and the course does not grant certification. Atlantis also offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training with pages for Tulsa, Oklahoma City, Wichita, Denver, Salt Lake City, Billings, Casper, Williston and Midland, and AWS CWI exam prep with pages for Tulsa, Denver and Salt Lake City.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Tulsa, Denver or Salt Lake City?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Tulsa, Denver, Salt Lake City or anywhere else in the Mountain and Plains states; Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. The API exam-prep courses are online and self-paced with instructor Q&A, and API runs the examinations at Prometric test centres.

faq.q: I inspect tank batteries in the Permian. Is API 653 the right certification?
faq.a: It depends on what you inspect. API 653 is written for aboveground tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, API 12C, while production tanks are usually built to API Specification 12F or 12D. If your work is mostly field tanks, API 653 still teaches you the methods, but check whether your employer or regulator asks for it. Terminal and refinery tank work is where API 653 is most clearly required.

faq.q: Does Oklahoma require API 653 for tanks at Cushing?
faq.a: Oklahoma's aboveground storage tank rules at OAC 165:26 adopt API Standard 653, Fifth Edition, by reference and exclude tanks used in exploration or production. Breakout tanks on pipeline systems are also covered by federal rules at 49 CFR 195.432, which require inspection according to API 653 and do not allow its risk-based internal interval. Which rule governs a given tank depends on how it is connected and operated.

faq.q: The nearest Prometric centre is hours away. What can I do?
faq.a: Book your seat as soon as your exam authorisation arrives, because seats within a window go first-come, first-served. API 580 can be taken by remote proctoring; API 510, API 570 and API 653 cannot. API also says it may arrange a special testing site when at least 50 applicants have no testing centre within 200 miles.

faq.q: I work at a gas processing plant. Should I take API 510 or API 570?
faq.a: Gas plants are full of pressure vessels, from inlet separators to amine regenerators and NGL storage, so API 510 is often the stronger fit for a plant inspector. If your role is mainly the plant's piping circuits, including amine and cryogenic lines, start with API 570. Many plant inspectors eventually hold both, and holders of either qualify automatically for API 580.

faq.q: Does wet hydrogen sulfide damage come up in API exam preparation?
faq.a: Damage mechanisms are examined through selected sections of API RP 571, and the effectivity sheet for your window lists which ones. A recent API 570 sheet, for example, lists amine stress corrosion cracking and corrosion under insulation but not wet hydrogen sulfide damage. Study the listed sections for the exam, and read the others for the plant you work in, because sour service will matter there whether or not it is examined.

faq.q: Can a small inspection firm sponsor one or two inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. Sponsorship works for one candidate as well as for a group, and fees are quoted on request. Because the course is self-paced, the firm does not have to release the inspector for scheduled class days; the inspector studies around the work and sends questions to the instructor when needed.

faq.q: Does an API certificate let me inspect boilers or pressure vessels for a state?
faq.a: No. API certification shows that you know the inspection code, but state boiler and pressure vessel programmes decide who may inspect for the jurisdiction, and those inspectors usually hold state or National Board commissions. Many owner-user inspectors carry both an API certificate and the credential their state requires.
